title: How To CRUSH The Scandinavian Defense | The Sensei Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: e4, and the Scandinavian — d5.
We know how to play against the Scandinavian — we take it, and we've got
the knight to c3 coming. The queen recaptures on d5.
The knight to c3, hitting the queen.

The queen to d8 — the Bartholomew setup, a move that's gained popularity recently, a very solid system. The best way to play against it is very straightforward chess: first we should occupy the centre
with our pawn, and then develop naturally and actively. What does that mean? We start with d4, of course, then the knight to f3, the bishop to c4,
and so on — the knight to f3.
h6 — that's already bad, completely unnecessary movement. We can try to punish it by playing in a very principled manner.
We should start with the bishop to c4, aiming at the f7-pawn. g5 here is an interesting move too, but I like the bishop to c4 — develop the bishop, aim at the pawn; and if he plays a loose move,
this is flirting with disaster. Why? The bishop to f5 without e6 — now we're
aiming at f7. We should definitely play the knight to e5 — and look, this is serious. e6,

this is serious, let me think. There are multiple tempting moves here, and I'm going to teach you a really cool tactical idea. Not g4 — g4 isn't dangerous for Black, don't succumb to one-move-itis; g4 and the bishop to h7 does nothing. The move I'm debating is the queen to f3, but maybe we should just be Russian and disciplined and castle and forget everything crazy. The queen to h5 is interesting, but he plays g6, and I don't really understand the follow-up. I'll go on record and say the queen to f3 is a mistake, but I'll play it anyway, in the hopes he allows the tactic. He can take on d4, and after the queen takes d4 I had a cool follow-up in mind — but he allows the tactic. What tactic? To find it you break it into parts: first, you detect the pressure we're putting on f7; second, you note that if the king lands on f7 the pawn on e6 becomes pinned — therefore the knight takes f7, the king takes f7, and the queen takes f5. Tactics are pretty logical when you think about it: now we win a pawn, the king is in shambles, and we're completely winning. This concept exists in many openings, not just this one — I can show you fifteen examples of this knight-takes-f7, queen-takes-f5 business. I know it's scary, because our queen seems to hang and we depend on a tenuous pin, but remember: if you get scared, you can always move the queen back — he can't break the pin and take the queen at the same time — and the bishop is completely safe on c4, it can even drop back to b3. When I do a tactic like this, file it away, even write it down or photograph it, and keep a running record of interesting tactical ideas, because before you know it you'll get a chance to apply it. Now, the queen to d6 is a tilt move that walks right into a developing move with tempo — get the bishop out with tempo again, and now we don't need to move our queen at all, the bishop is perfectly capable of defending it. Then we castle and try to put a rook on e1 and smash through on e6; this is already essentially resignable, and what makes it worse is that Black can never drop his king back to g8, because that blunders the pawn on e6. The queen to e7. Where should we castle? It really doesn't matter — kingside or queenside is essentially the same — but since we're in an attacking mood, I'll castle queenside. Why not g4 for Black? g6 is the only way to stay alive, and not for long. Where should our queen go? Think of the queen as a supporting actress: people are always tempted by the queen to e5 here, but that's counterproductive — putting your queen on the front lines is like sending Napoleon himself to fight in the trenches; you want your general behind the lines directing traffic. The queen to e5 walks right into the knight to d7, a developing move that forces us to move the queen again — we want to keep the queen back, still pressuring the e6-pawn but invulnerable. If you want more on this, I wrote a chess.com article a couple of years ago literally called 'The Queen, a Supporting Actress,' full of attacks where the queen was kept behind rather than in the thick of it. The king to g7 is very impatient and blunders the e6-pawn — thank you very much, we gladly take the free pawn, and Black's position collapses; the bishop to e5 is a great follow-up, pinning the knight to the king, and a rook to e1 is great too — anything is winning. Yasser is the originator of this concept; he's the one who told me about it. Black is totally busted. We can play the bishop to e5, because in the event of a trade our rook gets free, but in the interest of disciplined attacking chess let's get our final rook into the game. He sets up an x-ray against our queen — but really, it doesn't matter how you play here as long as you make decent attacking moves. Once the queen goes to d8, the first thing that catches my eye is that x-ray — I'm obsessed with x-rays, they're valuable and can be exploited, but only if we get rid of the d-pawn, and we absolutely can: we push d5, a typical attacking motif, and if Black plays c5, which I expect, we shove the pawn all the way to d6 to entomb the bishop forever. It's an x-ray because the rook is staring at the queen through a bunch of pieces. He takes on d5 — the bishop to e5 was just as strong, everything is winning. When you're this far ahead there are often four or five winning attacking continuations; don't obsess over which one you or I chose, because chances are the other move is winning too — it's a matter of taste, though of course sometimes a move really is wrong. The knight takes, we take back with the rook, completely crushing, just demolition. The bishop to b7 — we can take any piece and win, but since the two knights defend each other, the best is to take the knight and then take the other knight with the rook, because if he recaptures with his knight we take the queen. Take the queen — elementary. We can bring the queen to e6; the bishop to b5 to trade the last bishops is good; a rook to e6, or the rook takes f6, all fine — anything wins, it's trap city, you could be deep Stockfish and you're losing. The simplest is the bishop to e5, trading off the last defender of the king, and the point is that we want to get a rook to the seventh rank, the fastest path to mate — which is what we do now: a rook to e7 with check. I'm playing quickly because it's so winning that at this level you should be comfortable converting these. The simplest is to keep the rook on the seventh, the rook to h7, and then the queen takes h6 is the immediate mate threat; the other idea is the queen to a3 followed by the queen to e7, infiltrating the seventh rank. The position is completely resignable, so now we go for our secondary idea, getting the queen to e7 with checkmate along the seventh — and, by the way, use the whole board, not fixating on two files: even the empty queenside is a springboard to swing your heavy pieces over to the king.
Checkmate. Cool stuff — a pretty simple game, and that's why I don't
really recommend the Scandinavian to
lower-rated players, because it
violates certain principles — you should be a minimum of around 1600 or 1700 before you even
consider it. So h6 is a mistake; the move here, I think,
and you should ask John,
is that Black should play the bishop to g4, in order to prevent the knight from
coming to e5; and the bishop to c4 should always
be met with e6, to blunt the bishop.
But that isn't what our opponent did.
h6 is a waste of time, and when Black is this far behind in
developing, he cannot afford a waste of

time. So, the bishop to f5, or g5, then e6 — and why is the queen to f3 wrong? Because the queen takes d4. Now White has two interesting possibilities: one a developing move that keeps the tension, one the tactical approach you already know. The slow move is the bishop to f4, and what really worried me was the knight to d7, which is dangerous because the bishop on c4 is a type-two undefended piece and our position starts to collapse a little — the knight takes d7 is possible, with a big development lead, but after the queen takes c4 I wasn't entirely convinced, though after we castle things are still very good. That's one approach; the other is still the knight takes f7, the king recaptures, we take on f5, and if the queen takes c4 we take the rook on h8. Now you might say, isn't this

really good for White, up an exchange? Well, I'm worried this knight gets trapped, and after something like g5 and the bishop to g7 I wouldn't want those complications, given how nice our position already was. So somebody proposed

castling — and castling really is the mature approach to the position, but I wanted to show you this tactical idea, after which it's game over. To prove the point that it appears across openings, here's a game from 1996, a Caro-Kann Panov: the bishop to f5, and Black plays the capture, which is bad — e6 is the move here — the knight to f3, the knight to e5, the queen to f3, played perfectly, the bishop to d6, then f5, and here White plays the knight to e4, the very move we wanted, then the knight to g5 with check; and beautifully, the queen takes c6 with check, and White simply castles out of the pin — the point being a rook to e6 hitting the f5-fork, and White went on to win the game.
